material_decisions.answer: The existing greeting format is `Hello, {name}!` and the feature must preserve that exact output when no punctuation style is provided.
material_decisions.why_material: A receiver cannot define default behavior or backward compatibility without a fixed baseline output.

material_decisions.answer: `punctuation_style` changes only the terminal punctuation at the end of the greeting. The comma after `Hello` and all words remain unchanged.
material_decisions.why_material: This removes the core ambiguity around what counts as punctuation style and prevents examples from drifting beyond the written rule.

material_decisions.answer: The caller may optionally provide a `punctuation_style` field. If the field is absent, the system uses the default behavior. If the field is present, its value determines the terminal punctuation.
material_decisions.why_material: The optional behavior must be externally observable at the request boundary so implementers know exactly when the feature is active.

material_decisions.answer: Supported `punctuation_style` values are `default`, `period`, `exclamation`, and `ellipsis`. Their outputs are `Hello, {name}!`, `Hello, {name}.`, `Hello, {name}!`, and `Hello, {name}...` respectively.
material_decisions.why_material: Supported values and exact outputs are required for implementation and pass/fail verification.

material_decisions.answer: If `punctuation_style` is provided with any unsupported value, the system must reject the request with the exact error code `INVALID_PUNCTUATION_STYLE` and must not return a greeting string.
material_decisions.why_material: Invalid-input behavior is a key omitted decision point that otherwise forces downstream invention.

material_decisions.answer: The handoff must include exact acceptance examples covering at least: no option provided => `Hello, Maya!`; `period` => `Hello, Maya.`; `exclamation` => `Hello, Maya!`; `ellipsis` => `Hello, Maya...`; invalid value such as `question` => error `INVALID_PUNCTUATION_STYLE` with no greeting output.
material_decisions.why_material: Exact examples make verification objective and expose any conflict between prose rules and sample outputs.

question.prompt: This answer changes the public behavior and test cases. Which punctuation styles must the feature support in greeting output?

options.label: Two styles
options.description: Support exactly two styles: `default` and one alternate style, which keeps scope small but requires you to name the alternate and its exact output.

options.label: Several named styles
options.description: Support a fixed set of multiple named styles, which is more flexible but expands API and acceptance coverage.

options.label: Caller-defined punctuation
options.description: Let callers supply punctuation directly, which is most flexible but changes the feature from a style option into custom output control.

transcript.answer: Several named styles: support exactly `default`, `period`, `exclamation`, and `ellipsis`. Their outputs must be `Hello, {name}!`, `Hello, {name}.`, `Hello, {name}!`, and `Hello, {name}...` respectively.

question.prompt: This answer changes the public interface and the default behavior when callers do not specify a style. How must callers choose the optional punctuation style?

options.label: Optional parameter
options.description: Add an optional `punctuationStyle` argument/property and default to `default` when omitted; this is the most conventional and easiest to test.

options.label: Separate entry points
options.description: Expose distinct APIs per style, which makes call sites explicit but expands surface area and duplicates acceptance coverage.

options.label: Config only
options.description: Select style through configuration rather than per call, which narrows runtime flexibility but may fit a centralized settings model.

output.answer: Callers choose the style by optionally providing a `punctuation_style` field on the request. If the field is absent, the system uses the default behavior and returns `Hello, {name}!`. If the field is present, it must be one of `default`, `period`, `exclamation`, or `ellipsis`, and its value determines only the terminal punctuation of the greeting.
